solution:
Aromatic ketones are the compounds in which the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group is attached either to two aryl groups or to one aryl and one alkyl group.

For example, acetophenone (methyl phenyl ketone, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_3}\)) has one aryl and one alkyl group on the carbonyl carbon, and benzophenone (diphenyl ketone, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-C_6H_5}\)) has two aryl groups.

Yes — phenyl acetic acid, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-COOH}\), is an aromatic carboxylic acid, but of the SIDE-CHAIN type: its \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group is not bonded directly to the aromatic ring, it is bonded to a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) group which in turn carries the ring.

The chapter defines this class explicitly and uses this very compound as its example: aromatic compounds in which the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group is not attached directly to the ring are called side-chain aromatic acids. (Contrast benzoic acid, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH}\), where the carboxyl group is joined straight to the ring.)

Ethanenitrile is converted into ethanol in two steps — hydrolysis of the nitrile to the acid, then reduction of the acid to the primary alcohol.

Step 1 (acid hydrolysis of the nitrile, section 12.5.1) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N} + 2\ \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOH} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

Step 2 (reduction of the carboxylic acid, section 12.9.7) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH}\)

Both carbon atoms of the nitrile are retained, so ethanenitrile gives ethanol without any change in the number of carbon atoms.

The reagent \(\mathrm{AlH(i\text{-}Bu)_2}\) (DIBAl-H) reduces an ester only as far as the aldehyde; the reaction is run at low temperature so that the aldehyde produced is not reduced further (section 12.4.3). Methyl propanoate therefore gives propanal.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-COOCH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}]{\mathrm{AlH(i\text{-}Bu)_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CHO}\)

Product : propanal (propionaldehyde). Methanol is released as the other product.

Treating an arene under high pressure with carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride in presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride is the Gatterman-Koch formylation (section 12.4.3), which introduces a \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group into the ring. The methyl group of toluene is ring-activating and o-/p-directing, and the para product predominates, so the product is 4-methylbenzaldehyde (p-methylbenzaldehyde or p-tolualdehyde).

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + \mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{4\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-CHO}\)

Benzonitrile is hydrolysed to benzoic acid with a dilute mineral acid (section 12.5.1); the amide is the intermediate.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-C{\equiv}N} + 2\ \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

(Passing through \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CONH_2}\), benzamide, which is hydrolysed further under the same conditions.)

The product is benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid (phthalic acid).

1,2,3,4-Tetrahydronaphthalene is a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered ring, so BOTH carbons at which the two rings join carry benzylic \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) groups. Section 12.5.4 states that on oxidation of an alkyl benzene the entire side chain is converted to a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group; acidified \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) therefore destroys the saturated ring and leaves a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group on each of the two adjacent aromatic carbons. The aromatic ring itself resists oxidation and survives.
Formalin is the aqueous solution of formaldehyde gas. It is used for the preservation of biological and anatomical specimens.

Increasing order of boiling points :

ethane \(<\) formaldehyde \(<\) methyl alcohol

All three have similar (low) molecular masses, so the order is decided by the strength of the intermolecular forces, and the chapter gives that order directly : carboxylic acids \(>\) alcohols \(>\) ketones \(>\) aldehydes \(>\) ether \(>\) alkanes.

Ethane is an alkane, held together only by weak van der Waals forces. Formaldehyde has a polar \(\mathrm{C=O}\) group, so its molecules attract each other by the stronger dipole-dipole force. Methyl alcohol has an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond and so forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, the strongest of the three, and boils highest.

Dry ice, that is solid carbon dioxide \((\mathrm{CO_2})\).

In the Grignard route to carboxylic acids (section 12.5.6) the Grignard reagent in dry ether is added to solid carbon dioxide. The \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is the reagent that supplies the carboxyl carbon, and being a solid at \(-78^\circ\mathrm{C}\) that sublimes rather than melts it also keeps the strongly exothermic reaction cold — so it is reagent and cooling agent at once.

\(\mathrm{CH_3-MgBr} + \mathrm{O{=}C{=}O} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\)

[Textbook misprint: the equation as printed is not balanced. It shows \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) with no coefficient, but the reaction as written requires THREE hydroxide ions: with one \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) the two sides differ by 2 H, 2 O and 2 units of charge, whereas \(\mathrm{R{-}CHO} + 2\ \mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2^{+}} + 3\ \mathrm{OH^{-}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}COO^{-}} + 2\ \mathrm{Ag} + 4\ \mathrm{NH_3} + 2\ \mathrm{H_2O}\) balances exactly in H, O, N, Ag and charge. The stem is transcribed as printed. The defect does not affect the answer, which turns only on the oxidation-number changes of the aldehyde carbon and of silver.]

A redox reaction is one in which oxidation and reduction occur together. Both changes can be seen in this equation.

Oxidation : the aldehyde \(\mathrm{R-CHO}\) is converted into the carboxylate ion \(\mathrm{R-COO^{-}}\). The carbonyl carbon gains a bond to oxygen and loses its bond to hydrogen, so its oxidation number rises from \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{R-CHO}\) to \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{R-COO^{-}}\). The aldehyde has been oxidised.

Reduction : silver is present on the left as \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) in the complex ion \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^{+}}\) and appears on the right as free metallic silver, \(\mathrm{Ag}\) (oxidation number \(0\)), deposited as the silver mirror. Each silver ion has gained one electron, so \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) has been reduced.

The electrons lost by the aldehyde carbon are exactly the electrons gained by the silver ions, so the two changes are two halves of one reaction. This is what tells us a redox reaction has taken place — and visually, the appearance of the silver mirror is the evidence that \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) has been reduced.

The strength of a carboxylic acid depends on how well its conjugate base, the carboxylate ion, is stabilised.

In acetic acid, \(\mathrm{CH_3-COOH}\), the alkyl group has an electron-donating inductive effect \((+\mathrm{I})\). It pushes electron density towards the carboxylate group, intensifying the negative charge already present on the acetate ion \(\mathrm{CH_3-COO^{-}}\) and so DESTABILISING it. (The chapter makes exactly this point in Problem 12.1 : a \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect of the R group destabilises the conjugate base.)

In formic acid, \(\mathrm{H-COOH}\), the group attached to the carboxyl carbon is only a hydrogen atom, which exerts no \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect. The formate ion \(\mathrm{H-COO^{-}}\) therefore carries no such destabilising influence and is more stable than acetate relative to its parent acid.

Because the formate ion is the better-stabilised conjugate base, formic acid releases its proton more readily and is the stronger acid. Its \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}\) is correspondingly lower than the value of 4.76 the chapter lists for acetic acid.

[Textbook misprint: the question is printed as "...in presence of ---." followed on the next line by "KOH in ethylene glycol ?". The dashes are a stray placeholder left in the text; the reagent intended is the KOH in ethylene glycol named on the following line, which is the Wolf-Kishner condition given in section 12.8.3. Transcribed exactly as printed.]

Hydrazine followed by heating with potassium hydroxide in the high boiling solvent ethylene glycol is the Wolf-Kishner reduction (section 12.8.3). It replaces the carbonyl oxygen by two hydrogen atoms, so cyclopentanone is reduced to cyclopentane.

Step 1 — nucleophilic addition-elimination with hydrazine gives the hydrazone (Table 12.7) :

cyclopentanone \(+\ \mathrm{NH_2-NH_2} \longrightarrow\) cyclopentanone hydrazone \(+\ \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 2 — the hydrazone is heated with \(\mathrm{KOH}\) in ethylene glycol and loses nitrogen :

cyclopentanone hydrazone \(\xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{KOH}\ /\ \text{ethylene glycol}}\) cyclopentane \(+\ \mathrm{N_2}\)

So the action of hydrazine on cyclopentanone in presence of KOH in ethylene glycol is to reduce the \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group to a \(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\) group, giving cyclopentane and nitrogen gas.

An aldehyde adds one molecule of a monohydric alcohol in presence of dry hydrogen chloride to give the unstable hemiacetal, which adds a second molecule of the alcohol to give the stable gem-dialkoxy compound, the acetal (section 12.8.2 c). With methanol as the alcohol, acetaldehyde gives acetaldehyde dimethyl acetal.

Step 1 :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3-OH} \xrightarrow[\text{dil. HCl}]{\text{dry HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-OCH_3}\)  (hemiacetal, unstable)

Step 2 :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3-OH} \xrightarrow[\text{dil. HCl}]{\text{dry HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(OCH_3)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)  (acetal, stable)

The product \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OCH_3)_2}\) is acetaldehyde dimethyl acetal, that is 1,1-dimethoxyethane.

A nucleophilic addition begins with the nucleophile attacking the positively polarised carbonyl carbon, so anything that lowers the positive charge on that carbon, or blocks the approach to it, slows the reaction down. Aldehydes win on both counts (section 12.7.1).

1. Electronic effect : alkyl groups have an electron-donating inductive effect \((+\mathrm{I})\). A ketone has TWO alkyl groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon, and together they decrease its positive polarity and hence its electrophilicity. An aldehyde has only ONE such group (the other position carries a hydrogen atom, which does not donate electrons this way), so its carbonyl carbon keeps more of its positive charge and is more electrophilic.

2. Steric effect : the two bulky alkyl groups of a ketone come in the way of the incoming nucleophile and hinder its approach to the carbonyl carbon. In an aldehyde one of those positions is occupied by a small hydrogen atom, so the carbonyl carbon is much less crowded.

Being both more electrophilic and less hindered, aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.

Propanenitrile is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C{\equiv}N}\). Hydrolysis of the \(\mathrm{-C{\equiv}N}\) group gives a two-carbon-plus-one carboxyl product, propanoic acid, but the form in which it is obtained depends on whether the medium is acidic or alkaline.

a. Dilute NaOH — alkaline hydrolysis gives the water-soluble SODIUM SALT of the acid, together with ammonia :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C{\equiv}N} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-COONa} + \mathrm{NH_3}\)

On acidification of this solution the free acid is liberated :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-COONa} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-COOH} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

b. Dilute HCl — acid hydrolysis gives the free carboxylic acid directly, with the ammonia appearing as the ammonium salt (section 12.5.1) :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-C{\equiv}N} + 2\ \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-COOH} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

In both routes the amide \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CONH_2}\) is the intermediate.

[Note : the chapter's section 12.5.1 gives only the ACID hydrolysis of nitriles. The alkaline route in (a) follows the pattern the chapter sets out for alkaline hydrolysis of esters in section 12.5.3 (b) — the salt of the acid is obtained first and the free acid on acidification.]

[Textbook misprint: the book numbers this item "vi." although the preceding item (the action of dilute NaOH and dilute HCl on propanenitrile) is already numbered "vi." — block 3 of the exercise runs i, ii, iii, iv, v, vi, vi. This question is the SECOND of the two, and should have been numbered vii. It is referenced here as vi-b so the two stay distinct.]

The three acids are, in the order drawn : cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (an all-carbon ring), oxane-2-carboxylic acid (tetrahydropyran-2-carboxylic acid — the ring oxygen sits on the carbon that itself carries the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group) and oxane-3-carboxylic acid (tetrahydropyran-3-carboxylic acid — the ring oxygen is one carbon further away from \(\mathrm{-COOH}\)).

Increasing order of acidic strength :

cyclohexanecarboxylic acid \(<\) oxane-3-carboxylic acid \(<\) oxane-2-carboxylic acid

Justification. As the chapter shows with the haloacetic acids (Table 12.8), an electronegative atom exerts an electron-withdrawing inductive effect \((-\mathrm{I})\) which pulls electron density away from the carboxylate group, diffuses its negative charge, stabilises the conjugate base and therefore strengthens the acid.

- Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid has no electronegative atom in the ring at all, only carbon and hydrogen, so its carboxylate gets no such stabilisation. It is the weakest of the three.
- Both oxane acids carry a ring oxygen, which is strongly electronegative and withdraws electrons by \(-\mathrm{I}\), so both are stronger than the all-carbon acid.
- The inductive effect is transmitted through the sigma bonds and weakens sharply with every bond it has to travel. In oxane-2-carboxylic acid the oxygen is bonded to the very carbon that bears the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group, so it acts across one bond only; in oxane-3-carboxylic acid it is one carbon further away and its effect on the carboxylate is correspondingly weaker.

Hence the acid with the oxygen next to the carboxyl group is the strongest, and the one with no oxygen the weakest.

a. Cannizzaro reaction

This reaction is given ONLY by aldehydes having no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atom. On heating with concentrated alkali such an aldehyde undergoes self-oxidation and reduction — a disproportionation. One molecule of the aldehyde is reduced to the corresponding alcohol while, at the same time, a second molecule is oxidised to the salt of the carboxylic acid.

For example, formaldehyde with 50% sodium hydroxide gives methanol and sodium formate :

\(2\ \mathrm{H-CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-OH} + \mathrm{H-COONa}\)

An aldehyde that has an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen cannot do this — it undergoes aldol condensation with alkali instead.

Cross Cannizzaro reaction : when a mixture of formaldehyde and a non-enolisable aldehyde is treated with a strong base, the formaldehyde is the one oxidised (to formate, and to formic acid on acidification) while the other aldehyde is reduced to the alcohol. For example, formaldehyde with benzaldehyde gives phenylmethanol and formic acid.

b. Stephen reaction

An alkyl or aryl nitrile is reduced by stannous chloride in presence of hydrochloric acid to an imine hydrochloride, which on acid hydrolysis gives the corresponding ALDEHYDE. It is a method of preparing aldehydes from nitriles.

\(\mathrm{R-C{\equiv}N} + 2[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SnCl_2},\ \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{R-CH{=}NH{\cdot}HCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{R-CHO} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

For example, ethanenitrile gives acetaldehyde :

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C{\equiv}N} + 2[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SnCl_2},\ \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}NH{\cdot}HCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{CH_3-CHO} + \mathrm{NH_4Cl}\)

a. Alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\), then dil. HCl and heat — the methyl side chain of toluene is oxidised right through to a carboxyl group (section 12.5.4 : on oxidation of an alkyl benzene the entire side chain is converted to \(\mathrm{-COOH}\)). In the alkaline medium the potassium salt is formed first and acidification liberates the free acid. The product is benzoic acid.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alk. } \mathrm{KMnO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-COOK} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-COOH}\)

b. \(\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}\) in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) — this is the Etard reaction (section 12.4.3). Chromyl chloride in carbon disulfide oxidises the methyl group only as far as a chromium complex, and acid hydrolysis of that complex gives the aldehyde. The product is benzaldehyde.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}\ /\ \mathrm{CS_2}} \text{chromium complex} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CHO}\)

c. Acetyl chloride in presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) — this is Friedel-Crafts acylation, which the chapter names as the route to aromatic ketones. An acetyl group enters the ring, and since the methyl group of toluene is activating and o-/p-directing, the para product predominates. The product is 4-methylacetophenone, that is 1-(4-methylphenyl)ethanone.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{4\text{-}CH_3-C_6H_4-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

a. The structure is a six-membered all-carbon ring carrying a \(\mathrm{{>}C{=}O}\) group, with a methyl group on the ring carbon two positions away from the carbonyl carbon. Numbering the ring from the carbonyl carbon (which must get the lowest locant, as it is the principal functional group) and going round in the direction that reaches the substituent sooner puts the carbonyl at C-1 and the methyl at C-3.

IUPAC name : 3-methylcyclohexan-1-one (3-methylcyclohexanone).

b. The structure is two carboxyl groups joined directly to each other, \(\mathrm{HOOC-COOH}\) — a two-carbon chain in which both carbons are carboxyl carbons. The parent chain of two carbons is 'eth-', and two \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) groups make it a dioic acid.

IUPAC name : ethanedioic acid (common name oxalic acid).

The bromine is replaced by a carboxyl group through a Grignard reagent and dry ice (section 12.5.6). Three steps :

Step 1 — form the Grignard reagent. p-Bromoisopropylbenzene is treated with magnesium turnings in dry ether :

\(\mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}Br} + \mathrm{Mg} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}MgBr}\)

Step 2 — add the Grignard reagent to solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) in dry ether. The carbon of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) becomes the carboxyl carbon and a complex, the magnesium salt, is formed :

\(\mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}MgBr} + \mathrm{O{=}C{=}O} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}COOMgBr}\)

Step 3 — hydrolyse the complex with dilute acid to liberate the free acid :

\(\mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}COOMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. HCl}} \mathrm{4\text{-}(CH_3)_2CH{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH} + \mathrm{Mg(Br)OH}\)

The product is p-isopropylbenzoic acid (4-isopropylbenzoic acid).

Cyclohexanone has \(\alpha\)-hydrogen atoms on the two carbons flanking its carbonyl group, so it undergoes aldol condensation with dilute alkali; the chapter notes that a ketone with at least two \(\alpha\)-hydrogens gives an \(\alpha\),\(\beta\)-unsaturated ketone (section 12.8.2 g).

Step 1 — addition. Dilute alkali removes an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen from one molecule of cyclohexanone; the carbanion so formed attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule of cyclohexanone. The product is the \(\beta\)-hydroxy ketone (a ketol), 2-(1-hydroxycyclohexyl)cyclohexan-1-one :

2 cyclohexanone \(\xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}}\) 2-(1-hydroxycyclohexyl)cyclohexan-1-one

Step 2 — elimination. On warming, the ketol loses a molecule of water between the carbon carrying the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group and the neighbouring \(\alpha\)-carbon, giving the \(\alpha\),\(\beta\)-unsaturated ketone :

2-(1-hydroxycyclohexyl)cyclohexan-1-one \(\xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta}\) 2-(cyclohex-1-en-1-yl)cyclohexan-1-one

The two steps together — nucleophilic addition followed by elimination of water — constitute the aldol condensation of cyclohexanone.
